title: Divorce, permitted not loved
hookLine: permitted but disliked, with waiting periods and kindness

lines: WILL YOU GIVE BACK HIS GARDEN?
A MARRIAGE ENDS WITHOUT A VILLAIN.
cards: A woman comes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about her husband, Thabit ibn Qays, and she starts by defending him. I don't fault him, she says, not his character and not his faith. But she can't stay.
She's afraid that if she stays, she'll fall short of what she owes in the marriage. The Prophet doesn't lecture her. He asks one practical question: will you give him back his garden?
The garden was his gift to her. Yes, she says. So he tells Thabit to take the garden back and let her go.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, a marriage ends without a villain. Today's word: talaq.

teach.b: Talaq is divorce, and in Islamic law the husband's release of the marriage. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud says that of the things Allah has permitted, the one He dislikes most is divorce.
Hadith scholars have debated its chain. Some readers hear the same in the verses themselves: a door that exists, not meant to be swung lightly. Next, what comes before it.

Surah four says that when a breach is feared between husband and wife, an arbiter is to be appointed from his family and an arbiter from hers, and if they want to set things right, Allah will bring them together.

Talk first, with people who love both sides. Then, how the door is built. Surah two, in Pickthall's translation: "Divorce must be pronounced twice and then (a woman) must be retained in honour or released in kindness."
Each of those first two times, there is a waiting period, and during it the couple can come back together. Room to cool off, and at the end, either way, kindness.
The same verse forbids taking back what was given to her, with one exception, the story from the hook: when the wife asks to leave and returns the gift, it has its own name, khul'.

teach.h: SHE CAN SEEK HER RELEASE, TOO.
teach.b: She can seek her release too. The schools differ on details, including what happens when someone says the word three times at once.
Permitted, because sometimes a marriage can't go on. Not loved, because it's still a breaking. And even the breaking has manners.

how: Muslim couples in difficulty are encouraged to seek reconciliation, for example through family members or an imam, before divorce; a divorce is followed by a waiting period during which the couple may reconcile, and a wife may seek a release of her own, called khul'.

o: a vow a couple makes never to separate, whatever happens
divorce: permitted but disliked, ended in kindness when it must be
the waiting time a widow keeps after her husband dies

s: it permits it, with arbiters first, waiting periods, and parting in kindness.
a wife can seek to end the marriage herself
khul': Thabit ibn Qays's wife returned his garden and was released.
in surah two, the first pronouncements leave room to return
pronounced twice, each time with a waiting period and a way back, then released in kindness.

games.q: a woman tells the Prophet she has no complaint about her husband's character or faith, but she can't stay. what does he do?
o: tell her she has no reason, so she must stay.
ask if she'll give back the garden he gave her.
send her husband away in disgrace.
games.why: she agreed to return the garden, and he told Thabit to take it and let her go. no villain, and a way out.

practice: Bring to mind something that has ended for you, or needs to, and ask: could I leave it without making the other side a villain, with a thank-you, an apology, an honest goodbye?
Let one kind sentence form; if you pray, you can ask for gentleness in endings.

wordCard.voice: Talaq. Divorce in Islam: permitted but disliked, with arbiters first, waiting periods, a way back, and parting in kindness. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: release; in law, divorce by the husband.

carryVoice: Your line: permitted, not loved. Even an ending can be kind. Back tomorrow, same hill.
